newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Army sex accusers attacked by defense.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Army sex accusers attacked by defense.

text.p: Defence lawyers for the Army's highest-ranking enlisted man on Thursday sharply attacked the credibility of two women who have accused him of sexual misconduct.

The aggressive counterpunch came at a hearing to determine if Sergeant Major of the Army Gene McKinney should be court-martialed on 18 charges involving four service women, including indecent assault, adultery and obstruction of justice.

McKinney, 46, a high-profile advocate for the Army's enlisted soldiers, could be jailed for up to 45 years if convicted on all counts in the latest in a series of sex scandals that have rocked the armed services.

During a combative cross examination of one of the women, lawyers portrayed her as a struggling soldier who fabricated charges against four other superiors, three of whom, like McKinney, are African American.

They also suggested she went to see McKinney on two occasions after he allegedly hugged and kissed her against her will, including one episode in which she said he rubbed his erect penis against her torso inside his Pentagon office.
The Army has asked that the woman's name be withheld because she is in a witness protection programme.
One of the woman's superiors, Master Sgt. John H. Sims, testified the accuser "wasn't cutting the mustard" in her role in a special ceremonial platoon that guards the tomb of the unknown soldier.
"We had a lot of problems with her," Sims told defence lawers in the hearing. "She wasn't cutting the mustard, sir."

Defence lawyers also questioned an army sergeant in Colorado who said he didn't believe the story told by another of McKinney's accusers, Navy Petty Officer Johnna Vinson, who said McKinney propositioned her in a hotel lobby during a 1996 training course.
Sgt. John Hulsey, who worked with Vinson at the course, was questioned over the telephone.

"She (Vinson) told me Sgt. Maj. McKinney had asked her to come up to his room," Hulsey said. "I did not believe her when she told me that. Nonetheless, I had an obligation, and I asked her if she reported it. She said no, that it wasn't that serious."
Vinson, like two other alleged victims, came forward after a fourth alleged victim, retired Sgt. Maj. Brenda Hoster, took her story to the national media in February.
Fending off questions about why she kept silent on McKinney's groping and sexual advances for nearly two years, the accuser said, "I thought that it would embarrass the Army."

"I was under the assumption I was the only one experiencing these problems," the woman said. "I didn't want to create headlines saying 'Soldier attacked at Lincoln Memorial by Sergeant Major of the Army.'"
The woman said McKinney's most aggressive pursuit of her took place near the famous monument in Washington.
